title: Vision-Language-Action Models
blurb: Tests how VLAs turn actions into tokens, the three architectural families and their trade-offs, why internet pretraining transfers to robot actions, action discretisation and its precision cost, latency limits, and how a modality ablation shows a model uses both inputs.

refLinks.label: §61.2.2 Why Internet Pretraining Transfers to Robot Actions

questions.prompt: What insight makes RT-2-style VLAs work?
options: Robots need a new architecture designed only for motor control.
Language models can drive motors directly without any fine-tuning.
Actions must be predicted by a separate network from the language model.
Predicting an action token is the same job as predicting a word.
questions.explanation: Binning actions into extra vocabulary tokens turns control into autoregressive next-token prediction, using the same model and objective.

questions.prompt: How does a VLA differ from a multimodal chatbot that discusses what a robot should do?
options: It outputs an action token, not language.
It needs no image input, only the instruction.
It uses a different kind of transformer that can't produce text.
It only runs in simulation, never on real robots.
questions.explanation: Describing what to do and deciding what to do are different outputs, even on similar backbones.

questions.prompt: Why do π0-style models use a continuous action head?
options: Language models can't output more than 256 tokens.
Binning loses precision for fine, fast manipulation.
Continuous heads need no robot training data.
Discrete tokens can't be predicted autoregressively.
questions.explanation: A diffusion or flow-matching head outputs continuous actions at full precision, at the cost of extra machinery on top of the VLM.

questions.prompt: What does OpenVLA change compared with RT-2?
options: It removes the language input entirely.
It predicts pixels instead of actions.
It is open-weight, built on Llama.
It replaces discrete tokens with a continuous diffusion head.
questions.explanation: OpenVLA keeps the discrete-token idea with the same trade-offs, on an open LLM rather than behind an API.

questions.prompt: Why do VLAs generalise to new objects better than policies trained from scratch on robot data?
options: Its pretrained backbone already knows objects and phrases.
VLAs ignore the image and rely on the instruction alone.
Robot datasets are much larger than internet image-text data.
VLAs are trained with reinforcement learning only.
questions.explanation: Visual and language competence comes from pretraining. The action-conditioned part is small and narrow.

refLinks.label: §61.2.2 Why Internet Pretraining Transfers to Robot Actions

questions.prompt: Why do some VLA recipes add an auxiliary world-model objective?
options: It makes inference fast enough for a 1 kHz loop.
Predicting consequences may teach richer structure.
It removes the need for any action labels.
It turns discrete tokens into continuous actions.
questions.explanation: The theory is that predicting the next observation pushes the model toward why an action works. The chapter calls it active research, not standard.

questions.prompt: An action range of −1 to 1 is split into 256 bins. How wide is each bin? Give four decimal places.
questions.explanation: 2 / 256 = 0.0078. That is the finest resolution the model can express for this action dimension.

questions.prompt: Using discretize_action in Listing 61.1 with 256 bins and range (−1, 1), which bin does an action of 0.3 map to?

options: Clipping actions to the expected range before binning
Too few bins for a precise dimension, then blaming the model
Choosing the action representation before writing training code
Using 256 bins for every action dimension
questions.explanation: 32 bins for gripper force may be too coarse. The grid, not the model, can be what limits precision.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 61.2 say to store the full instruction text, not a task ID?
options: The model can't read numbers, only words.
The goal is to generalise across phrasing.
Task IDs take more storage than text.
Instructions must match a fixed template exactly.
questions.explanation: Varying the phrasing for the same task teaches the model to generalise across wording instead of memorising one string.

questions.prompt: A control loop runs at 500 Hz, but a VLA forward pass takes 80 ms. How do real systems cope?
options: Skip the VLA and use only the low-level controller.
Run the VLA slower, with a fast controller between.
Run 40 copies of the VLA in parallel.
Slow the control loop to match the VLA.
questions.explanation: The chapter says VLA inference usually runs below the control rate, with a faster controller filling the gaps. Chapter 64 covers fitting models on-device.

questions.prompt: Why scramble one modality at a time after training?
options: To measure inference speed with noisy input.
To augment the training data with harder examples.
To find the best learning rate for each modality.
To check the model really uses both inputs.
questions.explanation: A model that ignores the instruction would show no drop when it's scrambled. The ablation tests that directly.

questions.prompt: Scrambling the image dropped accuracy to 0.278, below the 0.316 majority baseline. What does that show?
options: The image carries no information on this task.
Without the right image, it does worse than guessing.
Scrambling the image corrupts the instruction too.
The model ignores the image entirely.
questions.explanation: The model leans heavily on vision here. Scrambled instructions still left 0.618, above the baseline, so the image alone carries much of the signal.

questions.prompt: Does the asymmetry show that vision always matters more than language for VLAs?
options: Yes, since images contain more bytes than instructions.
No, since the ablation was run on training data.
No. It's specific to this synthetic task.
Yes. Vision always dominates action prediction.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls it task-specific. That is the reason to run the ablation rather than assume.

bookExercises.prompt: State the "embarrassingly simple" insight that makes VLA models work, connecting next-token prediction for language to next-action prediction.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A transformer predicting the next language token and a transformer predicting the next action token are doing the same underlying computation. If an action can be represented as a discrete token from a fixed vocabulary, "predict what to do next" becomes just another instance of autoregressive next-token prediction, identical in mechanism to how a chatbot predicts the next word.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three architectural families for representing actions (discrete tokens, open-weight discrete backbones, continuous heads) and state one trade-off for each.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discrete action tokens (RT-2): reuses the entire LLM stack unchanged, but loses precision to binning. Open-weight discrete backbones (OpenVLA): same precision trade-off, but inspectable/fine-tunable by anyone. Continuous action heads (π0): full continuous precision, better for smooth/fast or multi-modal-solution tasks, but requires a separate action-generation mechanism bolted onto the VLM.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's ablation results (instruction-scrambled 0.618, image-scrambled 0.278, baseline 0.316), explain why the image-scrambled condition falling BELOW the majority-class baseline is more informative than it simply being lower than the instruction-scrambled condition.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The image-scrambled condition (0.278) falling below the majority-class baseline (0.316) is more informative than merely "lower than instruction-scrambled" because it shows the model is actively *worse* than a trivial always-guess-the-common-answer strategy when denied correct visual input, meaning its instruction-only guesses are actively miscalibrated, not just uninformed. Being merely lower than the other scrambled condition wouldn't by itself establish this; only comparing against the baseline reveals that visual grounding isn't just helpful here, its absence makes the model's guesses actively counterproductive relative to a naive baseline.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's full-accuracy result (1.000) alongside both scrambled conditions being well below it, explain what specific claim this combination proves about the model that the loss curve alone (converging to 0.0001) could not have proven.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The loss curve alone (converging to 0.0001) only proves the model fit its training objective well. It cannot distinguish between "the model learned to use both image and instruction correctly" and "the model found a shortcut using only one modality (or memorized training examples) that happens to also minimize loss." The full-accuracy-vs-scrambled comparison specifically proves genuine dual-modality dependence: since scrambling either modality independently causes a measurable accuracy drop below the full-accuracy condition, the model cannot be ignoring either one. A model that ignored the instruction entirely would show no accuracy change when the instruction is scrambled, and this pattern is absent from the measured results.

bookExercises.prompt: A team reports "our VLA model's training loss converged beautifully, it's ready to deploy." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say before agreeing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "A converged training loss only tells us the model fit its training objective. It doesn't tell us whether the model is genuinely using both the visual input and the language instruction, or has found a shortcut that relies mostly on one. Before considering this ready to deploy, run a modality-ablation check like this chapter's Worked Example: scramble the image and the instruction independently and confirm accuracy drops meaningfully in both cases, ideally compared against a majority-class baseline, since a model that's secretly ignoring one modality would show a perfect loss curve but fail unpredictably in deployment whenever that ignored modality actually matters."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 61.1 warns about picking too few bins for a precision-sensitive action dimension. Describe a concrete robotic task where 32 bins for gripper closure force would likely cause visible task failures, and explain what those failures would look like.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: With only 32 bins across the gripper's full closure range, each bin represents a fairly coarse chunk of the physical closure distance. For a task like picking up a fragile object (an egg, a piece of fruit) where the correct grip force needs to fall within a narrow window (enough to hold securely, not enough to crush), the nearest available bin might apply meaningfully too much or too little force. The visible failure mode would be inconsistent task success: the object is crushed on some attempts (bin rounds up to too much force) and dropped on others (bin rounds down to too little), even though the model's higher-level decision, "grasp this object," was correct, because the actual executed force came from an imprecise discretisation grid rather than a genuine modeling failure.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about $\pi_0$'s flow-matching action head as an alternative to RT-2's discrete tokens. Explain in your own words why a continuous action head is better suited to representing "several equally valid ways to grasp an object" than a discrete token vocabulary is.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A discrete token vocabulary must commit to one specific bin per action dimension per prediction. Even if two different grasp approaches (e.g., approaching from the left versus the right) are equally valid, the model's autoregressive token-by-token generation forces it toward one particular sequence of tokens, and averaging or blending between the two valid options during training can produce a token sequence that represents neither option well (a blurry compromise rather than a clean choice). A continuous flow-matching or diffusion head instead models a full probability distribution over the continuous action space directly, and can represent genuinely multi-modal distributions (two separate high-probability regions corresponding to the two valid grasps). At inference time, sampling from this distribution naturally picks one of the valid modes cleanly, rather than averaging between them the way a poorly-calibrated discrete-token approach risks doing.
